entities.summary:
Credit Suisse was Switzerland's second-largest bank and one of the world's major investment banks, founded in 1856 by Alfred Escher to finance Swiss railway construction. The bank's 167-year history ended dramatically in March 2023 when a cascade of scandals, client withdrawals, and loss of confidence forced an emergency acquisition by UBS for 3 billion Swiss francs — the largest bank rescue since the 2008 financial crisis and the end of Switzerland's 'two-bank' model.

Credit Suisse's 2020s collapse resulted from a remarkable accumulation of scandals: a 2021 executive surveillance scandal (the bank spied on employees), the Archegos Capital collapse ($5.5 billion loss, 2021), the Greensill Capital supply-chain finance collapse ($10 billion in funds frozen, 2021), fines for helping Bulgarian cocaine traffickers launder money (2022), and a conviction for failing to prevent money laundering (2022). The scandals destroyed client confidence; in 2022, clients withdrew $120 billion in deposits in a single quarter.

The Swiss government's March 2023 emergency brokering of UBS's acquisition for 3 billion CHF (compared to Credit Suisse's stated book value of 45 billion CHF) wiped out $17 billion of AT1 (Additional Tier 1) bonds — bonds that in normal restructuring would have been protected above equity. The decision to honor equity claims while wiping AT1 bonds created controversy across global financial markets and highlighted the risks of complex bank capital structures.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Credit Suisse's 2023 collapse — the largest Western bank failure since 2008 — demonstrated how accumulated scandals and loss of confidence can destroy even 167-year-old systemically important institutions, and its AT1 bond wipeout reverberated through global financial markets.
